summary: This defines a Song class, a blueprint for one track in a playlist app. Each Song remembers its title, artist, genre, and an energy level from 1 to 10, and can describe itself as a readable line of text.

lines.text: Fields are marked private so that outside code cannot change a song's title directly; this is called encapsulation, and it keeps each object in charge of its own data.
Energy level is an int rather than a String because it is a number you will later sort and compare songs by.

lines.code: public Song(String title, String artist, String genre, int energyLevel) {
lines.text: The constructor runs when you write new Song(...), and it requires all four values so a Song can never exist in a half-filled state.
The parameter and the field share the name title, so this.title tells Java you mean the field belonging to this object.
A getter hands out a copy of the field's value for reading, giving other classes access without letting them overwrite it.
This annotation states that the method below replaces one inherited from Object; if you misspell the method name, the compiler catches the mistake instead of silently adding a new method.
Every object inherits toString, and printing a Song calls it automatically, so overriding it turns unreadable output like Song@1b6d into a real description.
The + operator joins strings together, and the statement continues on the next line because Java ignores line breaks until it reaches the semicolon.
The int energyLevel is converted to text automatically when combined with strings using +.
